questions.stem: What is the role of chromosomes in a eukaryotic cell?
options: They control which substances cross the plasma membrane
They package long DNA molecules compactly with proteins
They make proteins by joining amino acids at the ribosome
They release energy for the cell by breaking down glucose
questions.explanation: Each chromosome is one very long DNA molecule coiled around proteins, which packs it into the nucleus and keeps it organised. Protein synthesis happens at ribosomes and energy release in mitochondria.

questions.stem: Why do chromosomes condense into short, thick structures at the start of mitosis?
options: Condensing the chromosomes doubles the amount of DNA in the nucleus
Compact chromosomes can be separated without the DNA tangling or breaking
Condensing the DNA allows it to be transcribed faster during division
Compact chromosomes can pass out through pores in the nuclear membrane
questions.explanation: Long, thin DNA would tangle and break if it were pulled apart, so it is coiled tightly before it is divided between daughter cells. Condensed DNA is largely not transcribed, and condensing does not change the amount of DNA.

questions.stem: Which description fits a pair of sister chromatids?
options: Two chromosomes that carry different genes for the same trait
The two strands of one DNA double helix held together by base pairing
The two identical copies of a chromosome joined at the centromere
The two chromosomes of a homologous pair, one from each parent
questions.explanation: After DNA replication in S phase, each chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids held together at the centromere. Homologous chromosomes are a matching pair, one from each parent, which are similar but not identical.

questions.stem: How do homologous chromosomes differ from sister chromatids?
options: Homologues are found only in gametes; sister chromatids are found only in body cells
Homologues carry different genes from each other; sister chromatids carry different alleles
Homologues carry the same genes but may have different alleles; sister chromatids are identical copies
Homologues are identical copies made in S phase; sister chromatids come one from each parent
questions.explanation: Homologous chromosomes, one maternal and one paternal, have the same genes in the same order but may carry different alleles. Sister chromatids are produced by replication, so they are identical unless an error occurred.

questions.stem: In which phase of the cell cycle is DNA replicated?
options: M phase
S phase
G1 phase
G2 phase
questions.explanation: S stands for synthesis: the DNA of every chromosome is copied, so each chromosome then has two sister chromatids. G1 and G2 are growth phases on either side of it.

questions.stem: Which list gives the phases of the eukaryotic cell cycle in order, starting just after a cell has divided?
options: M, G1, S, C, G2
G1, S, G2, M, C
S, G1, G2, C, M
G1, G2, S, M, C
questions.explanation: A new cell grows (G1), replicates its DNA (S), prepares for division (G2), divides its nucleus by mitosis (M) and then divides its cytoplasm by cytokinesis (C).

questions.stem: A cell is making new organelles and proteins and growing in size, but its DNA has not yet been copied. Which phase is it in?
options: G2
S
Metaphase
G1
questions.explanation: G1 is the first growth phase, before DNA replication. A cell in G2 has already replicated its DNA, and metaphase is part of mitosis.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes interphase?
options: It includes only the phase in which the cell replicates its DNA
It includes G1, S and G2 and takes up most of the cell cycle
It is the short phase in which chromosomes line up at the equator
It is the phase in which the cytoplasm divides into two cells
questions.explanation: Interphase is made up of G1, S and G2. It is the longest part of the cycle, in which the cell grows, replicates its DNA and prepares to divide. Chromosomes lining up is metaphase, and cytoplasm division is cytokinesis.

questions.stem: A human body cell in G1 has 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes and chromatids does it have at the end of G2?
options: 46 chromosomes, made of 46 chromatids
23 chromosomes, made of 46 chromatids
46 chromosomes, made of 92 chromatids
92 chromosomes, made of 92 chromatids
questions.explanation: Replication in S phase copies each chromosome into two sister chromatids that stay joined at the centromere, so the count stays at 46 chromosomes but there are 92 chromatids. The chromatids become separate chromosomes only in anaphase.

questions.stem: A cell's DNA content is measured through one cell cycle. It stays constant, then doubles over several hours, stays at the doubled level, and then halves. Which events cause the doubling and the halving?
options: Doubling: replication in S phase. Halving: division into two cells after mitosis
Doubling: growth in G1. Halving: chromosome condensing during late prophase
Doubling: chromatid separation in anaphase. Halving: replication in S phase
Doubling: protein synthesis in G2. Halving: breakdown of the nuclear membrane
questions.explanation: DNA content doubles gradually as the DNA is copied in S phase. It halves when the replicated chromosomes are shared between two nuclei and the cell divides. Separating chromatids in anaphase moves DNA but does not change the total in the cell until it divides.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of mitosis followed by cytokinesis in a multicellular organism?
options: Producing genetically different gametes for sexual reproduction
Halving the chromosome number so that later fertilisation can restore it
Creating new combinations of alleles by exchanging chromosome sections
Producing genetically identical cells for growth, repair and replacement
questions.explanation: Mitosis gives two daughter cells with the same chromosomes as the parent cell, so it is used for growth, repair and replacing cells. Halving the chromosome number and making varied gametes are features of meiosis.

questions.stem: In which sub-phase of mitosis do the chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell?
options: Metaphase
Prophase
Anaphase
Telophase
questions.explanation: In metaphase the chromosomes are attached to spindle fibres at their centromeres and line up across the equator of the cell. In anaphase the chromatids then separate.

questions.stem: Which events happen during prophase of mitosis?
options: Nuclear membranes re-form around two sets of chromosomes
The cell membrane pinches inwards to divide the cytoplasm
Chromosomes condense, the nuclear membrane breaks down and the spindle forms
Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles of the cell
questions.explanation: Prophase is the first stage of mitosis: chromosomes become visible as they condense, the nuclear envelope breaks down and the spindle starts to form. Chromatids separate in anaphase, and nuclei re-form in telophase.

questions.stem: During anaphase of mitosis, what moves to opposite poles of the cell?
options: The two strands of each DNA double helix
The sister chromatids of each chromosome
The two chromosomes of each homologous pair
Whole chromosomes, each with two chromatids
questions.explanation: In anaphase the centromeres split and spindle fibres pull the sister chromatids of each chromosome to opposite poles, so each pole gets one copy of every chromosome. Homologous pairs separate in anaphase I of meiosis, not in mitosis.

questions.stem: A micrograph shows an animal cell with two groups of chromosomes at opposite ends, new nuclear membranes forming around each group and the chromosomes beginning to uncoil. Which sub-phase is shown?
options: Metaphase
Prophase
Telophase
Anaphase
questions.explanation: Re-forming nuclear membranes and uncoiling chromosomes at the two poles mark telophase, the last stage of mitosis. In anaphase the chromatids are still moving apart and no nuclear membranes are present.

questions.stem: How does cytokinesis happen in an animal cell?
options: A new cell wall forms across the middle of the cell, starting from a cell plate
The nucleus divides into two while the cytoplasm stays as a single shared mass
The spindle fibres pull the plasma membrane inwards until the two halves split
A ring of protein filaments contracts, forming a furrow that pinches the cell in two
questions.explanation: In animal cells a contractile ring of protein filaments under the membrane tightens to form a cleavage furrow that divides the cytoplasm. Animal cells have no cell wall, so a cell plate forms only in plant cells.

questions.stem: Root tip cells are examined: 40 of 400 cells are in mitosis. If the whole cell cycle takes 20 hours, about how long does mitosis take?
options: 1 hour
2 hours
10 hours
4 hours
questions.explanation: The proportion of cells in a phase reflects the share of the cycle spent in it: 40/400 = 0.1, and 0.1 × 20 hours = 2 hours. Most cells are seen in interphase because it is the longest part of the cycle.

questions.stem: A drug stops spindle fibres from forming. Cells treated with it enter mitosis. At which stage will most of them be stopped, and why?
options: During telophase, because nuclear membranes need spindle fibres to re-form
During cytokinesis, because the spindle is what divides the cytoplasm
Before anaphase, because chromatids cannot be pulled apart without spindle fibres
Before S phase, because DNA cannot be replicated without spindle fibres
questions.explanation: Spindle fibres attach to centromeres and pull the sister chromatids apart in anaphase. Without them chromosomes cannot line up or separate, so cells are held in early mitosis. DNA replication happens in S phase and does not need a spindle.

questions.stem: All eukaryotic cells come from pre-existing cells. Which observation supports this?
options: Cells can be assembled in a laboratory by simply mixing purified cell molecules together
Microscopes show that all cells contain the same organelles in the same numbers
Cells grow larger during G1 by absorbing nutrients from their surroundings
New cells are only ever seen forming when an existing cell completes the cell cycle
questions.explanation: New cells are seen arising only by division of an existing cell, after it has passed through the cell cycle. No one has observed cells arising from non-living material, and cells differ in their organelles.

questions.stem: How do the daughter cells produced by meiosis compare with those produced by mitosis?
options: Meiosis gives two diploid, identical cells; mitosis gives four haploid, genetically different cells
Meiosis gives four diploid, identical cells; mitosis gives two haploid, genetically different cells
Meiosis gives two haploid, identical cells; mitosis gives four diploid, genetically different cells
Meiosis gives four haploid, genetically different cells; mitosis gives two diploid, identical cells
questions.explanation: Meiosis has two divisions, so one diploid cell gives four haploid gametes that differ genetically. Mitosis has one division giving two diploid cells identical to the parent cell.

questions.stem: What happens to homologous chromosomes in meiosis I that does not happen in mitosis?
options: They split at the centromere in the first division
They line up singly across the equator of the cell
They pair up, then separate into different daughter cells
They replicate twice, giving four chromatids each
questions.explanation: In meiosis I homologues pair, may cross over, and then separate so each daughter cell gets one of each pair, halving the chromosome number. In mitosis homologues behave independently and are not separated from each other.

questions.stem: In a cell undergoing meiosis II, single chromosomes each made of two chromatids line up at the equator, and there is only one of each type. Which feature shows this is meiosis II rather than mitosis in a diploid cell?
options: The cell holds only one chromosome of each homologous pair
The chromosomes are lined up across the equator of the cell
Each chromosome is made of two chromatids joined together
The spindle is attached to the chromosomes at the centromere
questions.explanation: After meiosis I each cell is haploid, with one chromosome from each homologous pair. A diploid cell in mitotic metaphase would show both members of each pair. Lining up, two chromatids and spindle attachment occur in both processes.

questions.stem: Why is the genetic variation produced by meiosis and fertilisation significant for a species?
options: Mutations can no longer occur in the cells of genetically varied offspring
Some individuals are likely to survive and reproduce if the environment changes
Every individual becomes better adapted than its parents to the local environment
Offspring become genetically identical to the fittest parent in the population
questions.explanation: Variation means a population contains individuals with different characteristics, so if conditions change some are likely to survive and reproduce, and natural selection can act. It does not guarantee that every offspring is better adapted.

questions.stem: A species of plant can reproduce only by mitosis. A new fungal disease arrives. Compared with a related species that reproduces sexually, why is it at greater risk?
options: Its offspring have half the number of chromosomes, so they cannot make defence proteins
Its cells divide more slowly by mitosis, so it cannot repair the tissue damage the fungus causes
Its offspring are all haploid, so harmful recessive alleles are always expressed in them
Its offspring are genetically identical, so if one is susceptible they all are likely to be
questions.explanation: Mitosis copies the parent's genome, so a population produced this way has little genetic variation and a pathogen able to infect one plant can infect them all. Mitosis keeps the full chromosome number, so the offspring are not haploid.
